newsitem.title: USA: Denying China MFN would hurt US interests - Cohen.
newsitem.headline: Denying China MFN would hurt US interests - Cohen.

text.p: Denying normal trading status to China would damage U.S. strategic influence in Asia, Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Wednesday.

Saying denial of so-called Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status would hurt American economic interests, Cohen noted, "It is equally obvious that it would damage our strategic influence and interests.

"Our friends and allies throughout Asia would question our ability to carry our a coherent policy toward China and thus toward the region as a whole," he told a gathering of diplomats and business people in Washington. "And it would play into the hands of those who might wish to see U.S. power in the region displaced."
Cohen said the U.S. position on China would continue to be one of engagement, notably on such issues as conflict on the Korean peninsula.

As part of that policy, Cohen said the United States was building a relationship with China's military, including exchanges of military personnel, plans to work out procedures to U.S. Navy ship port calls to Hong Kong after it reverts to China and pursuing rules for U.S. ships travelling in the same waters as Chinese vessels.
He said he hoped to travel to Beijing in the fall, and noted that Gen. John Shalikashvili, head of the U.S. military Joint Chiefs of Staff, had visited last month.

Cohen's remarks on the importance of maintaining MFN for China were in line with the Clinton administration's stance on the issue. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright made similar comments to Congress on Tuesday.

Congress is considering whether to overturn President Bill Clinton's decision to renew China's MFN status for another year. Administration officials have said they expect a tough fight with lawmakers who want to deny Beijing the trade relation enjoyed by almost every other country in the world.

A group of conservative and liberal lawmakers worried about human rights abuses, nuclear technology proliferation, missile sales and the huge U.S. trade deficit with China, oppose renewing China's MFN status.
